utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom, especially to you, Mr. Thayer. Welcome back. We haven't seen you for a long time. Is the next witness ready to go?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: He is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. Then the next witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And good morning to you, Mr. President, Your Honours. It's a pleasure to be back before this Honourable Chamber. I think the last time I was here, Mr. Monkhouse was clean-shaven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not the only development that's taken place in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: A significant one, nevertheless. Mr. President, while the witness is being brought in, I can let the Trial Chamber know that the Prosecution will move orally now to withdraw two witnesses from its witness list as a result of our review pursuant to the Trial Chamber's instructions. Those witnesses are Witness 130, and Witness 191.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome to the Tribunal and to the courtroom. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer for the Prosecution is conducting now your examination-in-chief. He has the floor. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you please --

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please state and spell your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Your Excellencies, Your Honours, my name is Mikajlo Mitrovic. Do I need to provide any additional information? I am a retired colonel. I was born on the 22nd of July, 1955, in Zelinje, Zvornik municipality, Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm a Serb by ethnicity. I'm Orthodox by religion. I completed the technical military academy in Zagreb where I received the status of an engineer in electronics. I completed primary and secondary school in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And thank you for that information, Colonel. Do you recall testifying in this courtroom for a little over a day in September 2008?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. It was in the Beara case, and I was a Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, have you had an opportunity recently to listen to that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you attest that the testimony that you listened to was accurately recorded and reflected in what you heard?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the testimony was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, can you attest before this Trial Chamber that were you asked the same questions today that you were asked back in 2008 in the Popovic case, that your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter numbers 7406 and 7407, Colonel Mitrovic's prior testimony in the Popovic case. The former being under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Both will be received as exhibits. The first one under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7406 shall be assigned Exhibit P2258 admitted under seal. And 65 ter document 7407 shall be assigned Exhibit P2259. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have some associated exhibits to tender which are reflected on the Prosecution's list of exhibits. There are approximately eight of them listed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These eight documents will be received. The first one is 65 ter 2816. It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Registry will provide us with the document numbers. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, associated exhibits shall be assigned exhibit numbers from P2260 to P2267. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And P2260 is under seal. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A small technical problem. I wish to greet everyone. Mr. President, I just wish to turn your attention to the fact that the documents which are on the Prosecution list with 65 ter numbers 7408, 7409, and 7400 are already Defence exhibits as follows. D197, D199, and D198.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this information. I think you misspoke when you said 65 ter 7400. It should be 7410, if I'm not mistaken. Is that correct? Or are you referring to 7400?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7400, yes. At least that is what I have on my list, yes. 7400.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Registrar will check if this reflects -- is also reflected in our documents, and, in that case, we would withdraw the P numbers and leave with it with a D number. Mr. Thayer, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, with respect to the remaining exhibits on the Prosecution's list of exhibits, the four associated exhibits we do not need to tender. Three have already been admitted. We won't seek to tender 65 ter 169. In addition, in the last category, the first two exhibits, 2681 and 2682, we will not seek to tender either. That leaves the transcript of Colonel Mitrovic's 2004 interview. I anticipate that both parties during the course of his testimony will refer to it, probably put it up on e-court. I don't think we intend to tender the entire transcript. However, if the Defence seeks to do that, we won't object to that. But we will be relying on it. That leaves one exhibit in the non-associated category that was not on the 65 ter list for the Prosecution. It is a handwritten organisational chart of the security and intelligence organs in the VRS that was sketched by the witness during that 2004 interview. I do intend to use that with Colonel Mitrovic today. We've put the Defence on notice. I don't think they have any objection to us using that with Colonel Mitrovic, and I would orally move to add that exhibit to the 65 ter list of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that this is 65 ter 7415; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we should come to that document later when you use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I'll proceed with the 92 ter summary of the witness's prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: As a JNA officer, the witness joined the security organ in 1983 and served in various security and counter-intelligence posts until the war started. In 1985, he met Ljubisa Beara and the accused. Beara was the witness's second superior officer and served as deputy chief and later chief of the JNA Naval Military District based in Split. The witness would see Beara several times a year when Beara toured the security organs or summoned the witness to the command. During this period, Beara was a superior officer to the accused, who was chief of the Naval Military District's counter-intelligence group. In September 1991, the witness was wounded by Croatian forces, taken prisoner, and held for 45 days in solitary confinement, during which time he was beaten daily, not registered, and hidden from the ICRC. Following his exchange in November 1991, the witness was appointed chief of the counter-intelligence group of the JNA 9th Knin Corps, where the accused was his immediate superior and chief of the Knin Corps' security department. General Mladic was Chief of Staff and later commander of the Knin Corps. General Mladic and Colonel Beara knew each other from this time because the Knin Corps was part of the Split military naval district in which Beara served. When the witness joined the VRS in May 1992, he was transferred from Knin to Drvar and became chief of intelligence and security affairs of the 2nd Krajina Corps serving in that capacity until the end of the war. Although Colonel Beara had been the accused's superior prior to the war, the accused arrived at the VRS Main Staff earlier than Beara and became Beara's superior officer at that time. The witness, in his Popovic testimony, described the structure of the VRS intelligence and security organs, the relationship between the subordinate and security organs in the VRS and the reporting and transmission of information between them. He also testified about the relationship between the security organs and their unit commanders, the relationship of the security organs to the military police units in the VRS, as well as the tasks of the VRS military police units, the relationship between the security organs and the MUP security services, and the importance of not withholding information or secrets from the accused. The witness also testified that he holds Colonel Beara in high esteem, as an officer, and that Beara and the accused held each in high esteem. Tolimir and Mladic valued Beara's work. The witness also testified that he held Vujadin Popovic in high esteem as an officer. Popovic at one time served as a desk officer in the 2nd Krajina Corps intelligence and security department, and the witness recommended Popovic for the post of chief of the Drina Corps intelligence and security department. Finally, the witness also testified about information he had concerning the smuggling of weapons and other contraband in humanitarian assistance and also by parachute air-drops.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, I have some follow-up questions for you; some, in part, based on your testimony in the Popovic trial, and some based on your 2004 OTP interview. And before we get started, did you have a chance recently to also review the transcript of your 2004 OTP interview?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had a chance, in fact, to remind myself a bit of this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. The first topic we'll address this morning is your capture and imprisonment in September 1991. I know this is a difficult subject for you, so let's go through it first. As you testified in the Popovic case, you were taken prisoner by the Croats and mistreated the entire course of your imprisonment. I want to just focus on a couple of things you said in your 2004 interview. The first concerns, just generally, the training which you received as a JNA officer in the Geneva Conventions and the proper treatment of prisoners. Can you tell the Trial Chamber just a little bit about what kind of training you received in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Your Excellencies, in the introductory part, I said that I graduated from the technical military academy in 1979. And I finished it as an engineer of electronics. After that, during my work, I continued my education and when, in 1983, I was admitted into the security and intelligence service of the then-JNA and I was subsequently sent to Pancevo to the intelligence education centre where I completed the security school which lasted for six months. In addition to that, I had to take exams which lasted for two and a half years to obtain the rank of major. And after the war I also attended master's degrees studies of contemporary sociology at the faculty of philosophy in Banja Luka. During work, we had to undergo various kinds of training. There were seminars, lecture, and so on, and we had occasion to come across the provisions of the international law of war; that is to say, the Geneva Conventions. So I am familiar with them in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, was the training provided by the JNA, with respect to the international laws of war and the Geneva Conventions, something that was given only to members of the security services or was it training that was given across the board, shall we say, to JNA officers and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was given to all members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you testified in the Popovic trial that, in addition to being physically abused daily and being beaten and having tear gas thrown in your cell, you were also never registered by the ICRC and were blindfolded and hidden from them when the ICRC came to visit the facility. Do you recall that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I was wounded and taken prisoner. And in Sibenik, what I considered to be paramilitary forces, the ZNG, they first took me to a hospital. I was only semi-conscious due to my wounds. I was wounded in the head, and I still have pieces of shrapnel in my head and they still cause problems for me. I was also wounded in my leg and shoulder. There were many Croatian soldiers who were wounded and who were in the hospital and they started threatening me, so I was happy when they came and took me to prison because I do not think I would have survived if I had stayed at the hospital. In prison, I was in solitary confinement, number 79, as you said, and I had severe pain in my head, probably due to my wound. I never received any sort of assistance. That is to say, the assistance was reduced to daily beatings. In addition to physical mistreatment and mental torture, there were situations in which they would bring me food, tinned food, but not the tin opener, because they would say that I could use the tin opener to inflict wounds on myself, so that I would just leave tins aside and occasionally they would take them away. It is true that I would hear when the ICRC would visit, because I could hear that. It's a long corridor. You could hear sounds of conversation and noises, and they would take me somewhere. I was blindfolded, and they took me downstairs, somewhere, probably to the basement, but I could hear from the guards also that it was the ICRC. Then when there were attacks on Sibenik by the JNA, they always threw tear gas into my cell. All other prisoners and detainees would be taken to a shelter but they would leave me there and they would tell me, Let your people kill you, and so on. I was not the only one who was imprisoned there. Of course, there were other officers and there were also civilians who used to work in Sibenik who were in prison, but they were in a common cell as opposed to me. Before the war, I knew the prison warden and also the chief of the MUP. We used to socialise up until the time when fighting broke out in Croatia. It was normal socialisation. And it ended by me being exchanged on the 2nd of November, after 45 days in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Colonel, I want to go directly to the transcript of your 2004 OTP interview. This is P2258. And we won't be showing any part that needs to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Oh, I beg your pardon. This is 65 ter 2785. 2785. And if we could go to page 15 in the English. And this should be page 16 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I'll just read the question in English, and we'll see -- and you'll have an opportunity to read your answer in your own language in a moment. On page 15 of the English, you were asked the question: "And the treatment that you received while in custody, was that in violation, in your opinion, of the Geneva Conventions and the internationally recognised standards of combat?" And again that's page 16 now and we'll look at the answer. It's page 16 in both versions. And in your version, Colonel, we can see the question being asked about little more than halfway down the page. In the English version, your answer is at the very top of page 16. And your response, when asked whether the treatment you received was in violation of the Geneva Conventions, your answer was: "Yes, yes, because every time that an ICRC team would come for a visit, because the Red Cross would come and visit, I would be blindfolded, taken out, and taken somewhere to the cellar, because I could feel, you know, I was walking down and descending." You were asked if you were hidden. You answered, "Yes." And then you stated that you were only registered on the day of exchange. Is this transcript accurate, in terms of what your answer was at the time, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: If fully reflects what I said, and I believe I repeated most of it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We're done with this exhibit for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you were exchanged, Colonel, you testified about this in Popovic, you were exchanged for 50 soldiers and a major. Can you explain why that was, how -- how it was that 50 soldiers and a major were exchanged for one colonel?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: You see, it was my luck that the Knin Corps command knew of me being taken prisoner and probably it was for that reason that I stayed alive. The corps commander, or, rather, the Chief of Staff of the corps at the time was General Mladic. General Tolimir, who was a colonel then, was at the helm of the security department of the corps. At that time, I was the most important prisoner of the Croatian paramilitary forces following General Aksentijevic, who was captured in Zagreb, whereas I was captured in Sibenik. When I was released, I was told this story you mentioned which was that General Mladic and the Knin Corps command, before I was exchanged, twice scheduled me to be exchanged but I simply was not brought to the location. They only managed to release me on the third occasion. So in exchange, a major and 50 soldiers were released who had been taken prisoner in Sinj. That was simply my price. An exchange of prisoners, to put it in plainest and most vulgar of terms, is an exchange of goods. There is a careful weighing of who is worth what, and then an exchange occurs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, was your value based on your rank, on your position, or on something else?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably both, the rank and position. I really couldn't tell you how they decided on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's talk a little bit very quickly about some geography just to orient ourself. There are reference throughout your testimony to Sibenik and Split. They are both located on the coast of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's look quickly at an a map book.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, this is just a late addition to the exhibit list. We actually didn't think it would be useful to crank out another list to just add the map book. I've advised the Defence that we're going to throw up P104 and just look at a map very quickly. So if we could do that. It's P104, page 5. And if we could blow up the map just a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see this map of the various VRS corps in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And during the time that you spent as chief of intelligence and security affairs or chief of the intelligence and security department of the 2nd Krajina Corps, where did you spent most of your time? Was it behind a desk, or were you out in the field within your corps's area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: While working or serving with the 2nd Krajina Corps, for the most part, I was in the field. I also had to spend a certain amount of time at the command post at Ostrelj. I have to point out something, though. As a superior command, that is to say, the corps command, we toured our subordinate units daily. It was mainly the brigades and we visited the front lines. Occasionally, we also spent the night in the commands of those subordinate units; whereas, on other occasions, we returned to our command, to our base. But in any case, I used most of my time to be at the front lines, visiting our subordinate units; that is to say, the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we can see here on this map the 2nd Krajina Corps depicted in the west on the border of Croatia. In July and August of 1995, Colonel, generally speaking, where were you during that period of time, July/August 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: In July and August 1995, I was in the area of the corps. I'm not sure at what location exactly. It may have been Drvar, but probably not just Drvar. I was probably also at Grahovo and Livno axis, because, at the time, we fought the HVO which was trying to break through to Grahovo and Glamoc. I know that on the 27th of July, we lost both Grahovo and Glamoc to them. It was a chaotic period of our attempts to defend the corps's area of responsibility. Therefore, at that time, I was in the corps area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, it is perhaps a very interesting story we are listening to. I'm a bit concerned about the relevance to our case and the indictment against our accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is the purpose of this line of questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The purpose of this line which is now at an end, Mr. President, was just to let the Trial Chamber know where this witness was during the period of time of the events that are charged specifically, July /August 1995. Just to give you an idea -- Your Honours an idea of what he was up to. I thought it might be a question that would be in the back of your mind. You've heard a lot of other witnesses who were more involved and physically located near the events. So I just wanted to place that in some sort of geographical context for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, let's talk a little bit about the actual work that you and your organs performed during -- during the war. If we could start, generally, talking about the tasks of the intelligence organs. If you could briefly provide the Trial Chamber with how you would describe the basic intelligence tasks of the VRS intelligence organs.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the intelligence organs of the VRS, like any other intelligence service, primarily busied itself with collecting intelligence about the enemy and its forces. In times of war, it is done by reconnoitring at the tactical level. One needs to know where the positions and deployment of enemy forces is, or are. Next, we also surveyed radio communications and monitored movements of units and received information about the enemy from the -- from friendly countries through operative work, as well as analysing the media. The intelligence organs followed anything that would physically take place between the front line and the enemy and deeper into the enemy territory. Whereas, counter-intelligence organs worked on everything on the other side, that is to say, from the front line and into our territory. I don't know how clearly I am explaining this, but I hope you understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And although it might sound, at least as it is interpreted in English, a little counter-intuitive, what you described as counter-intelligence is work that was actually performed, generally speaking, not by the intelligence organs but by the security organs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I am not following. If intelligence organs received security-related information, they forwarded it to the security organs, and the other way around. If the security organs, through operative work, received intelligence information, they were duty-bound to forward it to the intelligence bodies. In that respect, they had a very close co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Understood, Colonel. When you say in your answer: "... whereas, counter-intelligence organs worked on everything on the other side, that is to say, from the front line and into our territory," that responsibility lay, essentially, with the security organs and not with the intelligence organs. Is that fair to say? That's the only point I'm trying to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Their area was from the front line and into enemy territory. That is the simplest explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So front line into enemy territory is intelligence. Front line back into your own territory is security. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to follow up on a couple of specific intelligence methods that you spoke about in your interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to 2785; 65 ter 2785.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, this is your 2004 interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we'll be going to page 21 of the English and page 22 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, here you've described in your interview some of the things you've already spoken about. The electronic reconnaissance, and that's just basically intercepting radio communications; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We monitored enemy communication. We had devices which made it possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in the VRS, was that done by professionals, amateurs, or both?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Both. Those who were in charge were professionals in the field. But we also relied on the knowledge and skills of ham radio operators.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. You also refer in your answer - and this is on page 22 of the English, and we'll need to go to page 23 of the B/C/S - to relying on information and intelligence gathered by -- from seized documents from the enemy as well as interviewing prisoners of war. Can you tell the Trial Chamber a little bit about the importance, in your experience, of information that was gathered from interviewing POWs?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Information gathered from POWs are, for the most part, credible. Like the information you may find in enemy documents. In addition to that, POWs could provide us with troop information, so to say. At least those of them who were plain soldiers could not provide any crucial information, but what is interesting for any command at the front line is to know the number of trenches manned by that many people who have those specific weapons. This may be very important if you're planning to break through the front line or engage in any other combat operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's focus just for a couple of moments on the tasks of the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 25 in the English. And this will be page 26 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can see in -- in English at the top of the page 25, and it's about the middle of your page. We can see in the interview, you say pretty much what you just told us a moment ago, that: "The security service was engaged in issues dealing with, or on this side of the front line, in other words, things that were happening on our own [sic] territory?" And the question was put to you: "So protecting the secrets of your forces then?" And your answer was: "Yes. The territory and the forces, yes." And then you go on and describe what counter-intelligence entails in general. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to focus on one part of your answer here, after you talk about counter-intelligence and security being involved in revealing, monitoring and preventing enemy agents and their activities in our territory and our units, a little further down you say: "However, there was also, in addition to that, the counter-intelligence protection of documents, plans and people." Can you just provide a little bit more detail, please, for the Trial Chamber about what you meant there? What are you talking about when you talk about "counter-intelligence protection of documents, plans and people"?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: The tasks of security organs are complex, and you specified a number of such tasks. Basically, such activities are aimed at detecting possible agents functioning in the area of responsibility of the units in question. There were such agents who, for different reasons, forwarded information to the enemy, be it by radio communication or through couriers. They would forward information on the deployment and situation in our area of responsibility and in our units. In that regard, security organs undertook counter-intelligence measures to protect their units. What does that mean? It means that those units should be kept safe so as not to be surprised by the enemy. Command posts had to be protected so as to enable competent people to work there. One could not have unknown and uninvited people moving about command areas. There was another measure in place, which was the protection of commanders, especially that of the corps commander. He was protected in his capacity as such. In his immediate environment, there could only be checked personnel, and this applies to couriers, secretaries, and all assisting personnel. We could not allow to have someone in that circle of people who had not been checked and was not to be trusted. Counter-intelligence protection of territory involves the following: One needs to control the territory to prevent any sabotage and terrorist incursions. There were such attempts and groups on a number of occasions, and not only in the AOR of our corps. Such groups can cause great damage. They can set up ambushes, kill personnel, destroy infrastructure and materiel resources. Those were the most important tasks, in addition to staff security. This means the participation of staff security organs in the decision making process of the command, in terms of certain operations, as well as information which has to do with managing the military police. Those were the principle tasks during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, it may be that you've touched upon this in the answer you just provided, when you spoke about, in your answer in your OTP interview about counter-intelligence protection of plans, what -- what are you talking about there, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, primarily any work and elaboration on combat documentation is carried out in the corps command in a specific room under certain measures. When that work is being carried out, first and foremost, no uninvited personnel is allowed in the room, including VRS officers who are not directly involved in the process and work on that future project or task. In other words, the number of personnel involved needs to be narrowed down so as to have a minimum number of people. Also, no documents may be taken out of that room unless strictly checked. Such plans were protected in that way. They were held in a separate safe in a room within the staff. Such rooms were guarded round the clock. Such measures were in place until the plan became implemented. The most important part of the process is preparation and elaboration of command decisions, in order to put together a plan. Once the plan is in its operational phase, then many things are no longer secret. That is it, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And understanding what you just said, that once the plan is under way and being implemented, necessarily certain information becomes known. Can you describe for the Trial Chamber what role the security and intelligence organs would continue to play during the course of an operation to maintain the secrecy of an operation?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the process of decision making all security and intelligence organs participate. Intelligence organs usual provide information about the enemy which are normal part of the corrected -- decision on the part of the commander for possible combat activities. And security and intelligence organs also provide the assessment of the situation in the field, whether the communications are working, whether roads are such that military convoys can travel. How about traffic nodes, are there any dangers for units of in the territory, and so on and so forth. So, more or less, these would be the duties. So a proposal is also given to the commander on how to use a military police unit. That is the proposal, and then the commander approves, or, rather, orders the use of the military police unit. That's the preparation stage. Security organs also say what are the security measures which all subordinate units must implement as part of the commander's order. So it is not my decision as the chief of the security but it is one of the points which is called security support, in order to prevent a counter-attack and anything else that might obstruct such an operation. So measures are outlined how not to communicate by radio or just through courier, not to use telephone lines, and so on, to step up reconnaissance in depth in the territory, to keep the plans where prescribed, not to carry documents to combat tasks if not necessary for the operation. Because our superiors would often put everything they had into their bag, all the documents they had, and carried them with them to the front. So sometimes they would lose them or they would be killed, and that was a way for information to leak. So, more or less, that was the role of security organs in the preparatory stage and during the carrying out of an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to what extent would the security and intelligence organs be responsible for monitoring the course of an operation to ensure that the security was maintained properly of an operation?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Intelligence and security organs participated in these operations. They monitored what was happening, in a way. They followed the movements of enemy forces, the situation in the territory. And it was always envisaged that you would have some forces as a reserve so that you could intervene possibly if a problem should arise in some section of the front or on a particular axis. And they were also at the command post. If it's a brigade, and if a brigade carried out combat activities, then they were most often at the command post of the brigade, together with the brigade staff. They were also with the units, if the units were those that carried out the combat operations, and so on. After that, an analysis would be made and one could see exactly where any problems or shortcomings may have occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, Colonel. Let's take a few moments and look at a sketch you drew. We spoke about this a little earlier. I think it will be helpful to have you explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 7415 on e-court, please. And we'll just work with the original B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I will be asking you to explain, in any event, so I don't think we need to put up a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At this point in time, I would like to ask the Defence if there's any objections to add this document to the 65 ter exhibit list? Mr. Tolimir, do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I greet everyone present. And may God's will be done in these proceedings and today and not according to my wishes. I especially wish to greet Mr. Mitrovic and wish him a pleasant stay among us. The Defence has nothing against presenting any document which points to anything that is incorrect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave is granted to add this document to the 65 ter exhibit list. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, if could you explain the title you've written across the top of this chart. It begins "nacelna ..."?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a general chart, organisational chart, of the intelligence and security system of the VRS from mid-1993 to the end of the war. But I added in brackets that it is possible that it was from 1994 onwards. Why? Perhaps Mr. Prosecutor might ask me that. Because, in that year, 1993 or 1994, there was a separation of the intelligence component from the security component at the corps level.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the top box that we have there, we see General Tolimir's name. And what have you written above his name there?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: In this general chart at the top of the pyramid is the intelligence and security sector which was a part of the Main Staff. At the head of this sector was the assistant commander for intelligence and security affairs. At the time, that was Major-General Zdravko Tolimir. Directly subordinated to this sector were the security administration of the Army of Republika Srpska which was headed by naval Captain Ljubisa Beara; and intelligence administration, headed by Colonel Petar Salapura. In the security administration, professionally speaking - and I emphasise this because there may possibly be a question later on who were the security organs subordinated to and how - professionally speaking, they were subordinated to corps security departments of all corps. So we have the security departments of the 1st Krajina Corps, the 2nd Krajina Corps, then third is the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Well, they were specific because they still had this intelligence and security department joined to the end of the war, probably because they were few and they were close to the Main Staff. And in numerical terms, they were few. Then the Eastern Bosnia Corps security department. Then the Drina Corps security department. The Herzegovina Corps security department. And also subordinated to the security administration was the counter-intelligence group of the VRS Main Staff. That's how it was called. And the Department of Security of the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska. These were the security departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go through these boxes that you've drawn on the left-hand side of the chart and put some names to the boxes. You started off with the 1st Krajina Corps security department. And you've abbreviated that 1 KK; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And in July 1995, who was the chief of the security department of the 1 KK?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: If we are talking about 1995, the chief of security in the 1st Krajina Corps was Colonel Stevo Bogojevic [Realtime transcript read in error "Bogovic"]. The department chief in the 2nd Krajina Corps was myself. The chief of department in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was the then-Colonel Marko Lugonja. Chief of department in the Eastern Bosnia Corps was Colonel Milenko Todorovic. I think his first name was Milenko. And the chief of the security department in the Drina Corps was Vujadin Popovic. I don't remember who was the chief of the department in Herzegovina Corps because there were several people in that position during the war. I don't remember who was last among them. And the chief of the security department at the Ministry of Defence was -- I'm not sure if he was a reserve lieutenant-colonel --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know his first name and the chief of the counter-intelligence group was the then-Colonel Petar Jakovljevic. These were the persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to stop you, because -- the interpreters didn't catch the last name you mentioned. Could you please repeat this name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Do you mean the Department of Security -- or, rather, which chief? Colonel Petar Jakovljevic was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was referring to the security department at the Ministry of Defence. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think his name was Pereula at the Ministry of Defence, yes. I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to clarify two other things. You mentioned, line 1 of page 26, "the chief of security in the 1st Krajina Corps was Colonel Stevo ...," and the family name was not correctly recorded. Please repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Stevo Bogojevic. Perhaps it said Colonel Milan Stevilovic on this page. He was the predecessor of Stevo Bogojevic. Perhaps that's what was recorded on the page. I didn't pay attention to that, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We need everything on the record. With these names, it is quite difficult to put everything correctly into the transcript. And you were talking about the chief of department, the Eastern Bosnia Corps Colonel Milenko Todorovic. You added one sentence to that which was not recorded. You said you are not sure if the first name was Milenko; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are right. I think that that was his name, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But? You're not sure about that, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not. I think that it is, but I'm not quite certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just two quick follow-up questions about this side of the chart, Colonel. The box that's the second from the bottom, you've used the abbreviation KOG GS - with what we refer to as the full banana on top - VRS. That abbreviation, I take it, stands for the counter-intelligence group of the VRS Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the last follow-up question about this side of the chart, you I think explained this in part. The third box down where it refers to the Department of Security -- well, let me put it this way. You've written department SRK OBP, and you've drawn a line from that box to the box containing Colonel Salapura's name. Could you just explain to the Trial Chamber why you've drawn that line?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, I drew this line because, as I said in my answer when I was explaining the general chart, it was only in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that until the end of the war the function of security organs and intelligence organs was not separated. It was one and the same department. Namely, to clarify, up until 1993, that is to say, since the establishment of the security system in the VRS up until at some point in 1993 and the arrival of naval Captain Beara to the Main Staff, that is the connection that I make, at least once he became the chief of the security administration, until his arrival, all the departments in all the corps were joined. They had intelligence and security personnel and character. After his arrival, a separation was made of these two functions, the intelligence one and the security one. This is why there are two lines here. One is connected to Beara. These are the security departments, whereas the intelligence departments are connected with Colonel Salapura. But as the department remained one for intelligence and security department in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, they had to submit their reports to Salapura as well. As the chief of security, I did not have to submit my reports to Colonel Salapura but exclusively to Beara and that's the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So when you use the abbreviation OBP in the box for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps' chief, literally what does OBP stand for? What does that abbreviation that you've used stand for?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: It's at the beginning, intelligence and security affairs. Intelligence and security system is what it says here. But this is intelligence and security affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We've got a couple of minutes before the break so I think we should be able to finish talking about the chart. And let's turn to the right side of the chart under Colonel Salapura's name. Now, the Trial Chamber has heard testimony already about the operation of the intelligence department. But, if you would, to the extent that you can remember, can you provide the Trial Chamber with the names of any of the corps chiefs of intelligence. If you can't remember, that's okay. But if you can, if you would provide the names for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to state some names. The chart is basically similar to the chart which relates to the security administration, their-intelligence departments in all corpses plus the 410th Intelligence Centre. I think it was seated in Banja Luka at the time, or perhaps Bijeljina - I'm not certain - and the 10th Sabotage Detachment. The chief of the intelligence department was Colonel Djuric. I don't remember his first name. I knew him. That was in the 1st Krajina Corps. The chief of the intelligence department in the 2nd Krajina Corps -- in the first one it was Colonel Djuric. In the second, it was Colonel Milan Atlagic. The chief of the 410th Intelligence Centre -- I don't remember the other people, as I didn't know them. The chief of the 410th Intelligence Centre was Colonel Cedo Knezevic. And the commander of the 10th Sabotage Detachment was Lieutenant Miso Pelemis. These are the names that I can remember from the intelligence branch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the name of the chief of the 410th Intelligence Centre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The chief of the 410th Intelligence Centre was Colonel Cedo Knezevic. That's what he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was it Knezevic or Knezovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first you said, Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, we can see that there's an arrow that points upwards next to these boxes indicating the various intelligence organs. Does that arrow mean anything?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it indicates for both branches what the reporting system was. That is to say, all the departments or the units which are listed here in -- on both sides reported upwards. And the horizontal arrow above the number, 358736, means an exchange -- an exchange of information between the administrations, between the departments, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 7415.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7415 shall be assigned Exhibit P2265, marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At this point in time, I would like to ask Mr. Registrar to provide us with the correct numbers of the associated exhibits used in the Popovic trial.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Having in mind Mr. Gajic's remark regarding the identical documents that were tended by the Prosecution, I have reassigned exhibit numbers in the following order: 65 ter document 2816 shall be assigned Exhibit P2260, admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for speaking slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 2818 shall be assigned Exhibit P2261. 65 ter document 2854 shall be assigned Exhibit P2262. 65 ter document 3324 shall be assigned Exhibit P2263. And 65 ter document 7410 shall be assigned Exhibit P2264. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And for the sake of the record, please give us again the D numbers of the three remaining documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just one moment. 65 ter number 7400 that was tendered by the Prosecution was previously admitted as Defence Exhibit D197. 65 ter document 7408 was previously admitted as D198. And 65 ter document 7409 was previously admitted as Defence Exhibit D199. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I take it the numbers, the P numbers, given to the three Defence exhibits are now vacated. Mr. Thayer, is this perhaps an appropriate time for our first break?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, it's, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Because I assume you are moving to another part of your questioning. We must have our first break now, and we will resume at 11.00. And the Court Officer will assist you during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning again to you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, you testified in the Popovic trial, and just, for the record, this was at pages 25141 to -42, about the daily intelligence reporting that went from the subordinate units all the way up to the Main Staff, and you also testified about how the Main Staff transmitted its information down through the subordinate units for your use. Was there a particular time of day by which your intelligence and security department, or departments when they got split, were required to submit your daily intelligence reports?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was as follows -- following: Informing and reporting is one of the more important aspects of the system of chain of command in any army. We were duty-bound to draft a report by 6.00 p.m. every day and send it from the level of the corps security department. We were supposed to send it to the security administration and its intelligence and security sector at the level of the Main Staff. Before 6.00, we needed to gather information from our subordinate units, that is to say, the brigades and regiments, by way of their reports, on the basis of which, we drafted our own. Those reports, for the most part, contained some standard points that were prescribed by the regulations, and most of the answers were rather typical in that sense. The first item was the situation at the front line. Next, combat readiness. Then the situation in the territory, as well as logistics and its situation in the unit and in the field. Then the state of morale in the unit and so on and so forth. All of those elements were contained in the report. In other words, the command would be send such reports to us and then to the Main Staff. As for our security organs, we received their information from our subordinate units about the situation in their respective units and what security issues they had, and such security issues could have been of different types. We also wanted to know whether there were any counter-intelligence problems and whether they were being addressed and in what way. We also wanted to know what the situation was in the units of the military police, in terms of training, equipment, et cetera. Those would all be parts of our daily reports that we sent to the Main Staff. The Main Staff did something that you mentioned in the sector part of your question. In other words, they sent daily intelligence and security information to the corps commands. Those were information bulletins about the situation at the level of the RS and the VRS. By nature of my work, I was unable to know what was going on in the East Bosnia Corps, for example, because I was all the way to the west. By the same token, I wasn't privy to developments in the Herzegovina Corps. We received such information from the Main Staff enabling us to see at least partially what the situation was throughout the territory and the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, page 34, line 5, we see you repeat the intelligence problems, whereas it should have been counter-intelligence, as interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, just to be clear about the different types of reporting that were going on, is it the case that there was a daily combat report which was issued by the corps command that went to the Main Staff, in addition to the daily security report that your department would send up to the Main Staff's security and intelligence sector? Were those two separate reports or are you talking about one report? Just so we're clear.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: There were two separate reports. But the command report also contained elements pertaining to the security situation. There was a standard item in that report, the title of which was: Security. Within that particular paragraph, there were always a few sentences stipulating what took place during that particular day at the corps, in terms of security, and it usually concerned general security, as regards the corps command. In the reports that were sent by the intelligence -- by the security department when we sent them to our administration, we were more detailed in them, providing more precise, for the lack of a better word, information about the security situation in the corps area, including counter-intelligence issues, as well as general security issues. I'm trying to say that there was a difference which was obvious only in that part in which the reports of the command were general in nature. There were no counter-intelligence issues specified in any detail. I can use an example to illustrate that. In the command report, perhaps it would be included that, in an X/Y area, an enemy operational position of -- was detected. And then in the other report that we sent to our administration, we specified in detail what the position was and what measures we would take to address it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in the -- in your interview with the OTP in 2004, and to save a little bit of time, I won't put it up on the screen, you mention - and this is at page 43 of the English and page 46 of the B/C/S, if anybody wants to look at it later -- you mentioned that the brigades within your corps had to brief the corps command twice a day on the situation in their area of responsibility, and that each corps had an operations centre with communication links with the subordinate units. Do you remember telling us that in 2004, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was. Each command post - and this goes for all armies in the world - there is an operational centre where all communication means are placed to communicate with the subordinate units. All subordinate units would channel their information to that hub regarding the situation in their respective areas. That operational centre monitored events and noted them and it included entire corps area of responsibility. Usually, such reporting was done twice in the morning and in the evening before 6.00 p.m. because I've already said that by that time we should have produced a report already. We also wanted to know how the night went in their areas, whether there were any problems. So the morning briefing was usually not of that much importance; whereas the afternoon reporting usually contained much more information and detail. That was the only difference. And we also received reports as needed, not only on those two occasions. If the enemy broke through our lines, the command of the corps was notified immediately. Also, if the enemy stepped up its activities, the command would be informed as well. The two particular briefings we addressed simply offered an overview of the situation in general terms up to that particular time of day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at 65 ter 2785 again, please. That is the transcript of your OTP interview. I want to follow up on this topic of communications and look at a portion of your interview in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we'll be going to page 81 in the English and page 85 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, just take a moment, if you would, to read in your language approximately from line 9 or so down to the bottom of the page. Just take a moment, reacquaint yourself with this portion of your interview, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In B/C/S, it would be, if I'm not mistaken, line 15 downwards; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Approximately. Maybe even up a little bit, line 9. But that's the general area. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Line 9 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I was referring to the English text. Line 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Mr. President. In English, yes, line 15, exactly. And we can stay on the one page in B/C/S but Colonel Mitrovic's answer in the English transcript goes to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, have you had a chance -- okay. I see that you're nodding yes. The -- you refer to this Neven communications system, this encrypted or protected system, and if we can - yes - go to the next page thank you. In the English, it's at the top of page 82. You state that: "All the corps were connected through Neven with the security administration with Tolimir." Can you explain what you're talking about there, how all the corps were connected with General Tolimir through this Neven system.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: This is correct. Excuse me. The Neven system was a computer system. It was a coded software that could only be used by the administration sector at the Main Staff and security departments in the corps. The communication was direct, and we could rely on it by using our codes to pass on information to our security administration. The system was rather simple to use. I believe I also mentioned that in our reporting we used the same code as was used by the corps command. The Neven system was to communicate between the security department in the Main Staff and its security administration. In other words, the different corps could not communicate using that system horizontally. That would be the best explanation I can give.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Let's turn to another topic now, and we'll stay with your interview for a little while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment. I have an additional question. Throughout the time-period from June to August 1995, did this system, this Neven system, work all the time, or were they -- were there any problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot be specific because July and August was a different -- difficult period for our corps. We were constantly in combat and had to move. I believe in August or September we abandoned the corps command post. Probably the Neven system was not in operation by that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you have specific knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't recall anything specific, but I believe that if we had to move from our command post, it affected the system. I no longer remember whether we were able to set it up later on. In that period of time, we probably reported by way of codes and the command line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You just told us that in August or September you - that means your unit - abandoned the corps command post. Could you be a bit more specific? What does that mean, in fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in August and September, we were under constant attack, and we lost territory. In late August and in early September, we abandoned our command post at Ostrelj because we were exposed to artillery fire on a daily basis. It was for that reason that we had to leave Ostrelj and go to Bosanski Petrovac, which is some 10 kilometres away. Later in September, when the Muslim and Croat forces attacked Petrovac, we withdrew toward Kljuc. In that period of time, so from August and until the end of the war, we no longer had a permanent command post. We simply set it up in different locations depending on where we happened to be. When I say that we set up different command posts, I mean to say that it was never a standing command post as it had been at Ostrelj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: After you moved to Bosanski Petrovac, did you set up the Neven system again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. But I don't think we were able to. I think we only used the code system. I can't say anything with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you recall if the Neven system was working at any other location where you moved with your command post after August or September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible that it worked when we were in Banja Luka later on. Basically that system resembles regular e-mail, only that this one is protected. You needed communications, and at that time, we could only use radio relay communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you have any information if at other command posts, wherever in that region, the Neven system was in place when it was abandoned in your command post? I'm referring specifically to the same time-period, from June to August 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it worked in Banja Luka, as part of the 1st Krajina Corps, because they did not move. I also believe, since the situation there was stable, it worked in the East Bosnia Corps, as well as in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, so all those corps which stayed within their areas. Since they didn't need to move, they probably could still rely on the Neven system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that clarification. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to follow up on your last answer, would you include the Drina Corps as one of the corps that didn't have to move outside their area of responsibility, as your corps did in August and September?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I probably would. As far as I recall, their command post was in Vlasenica and it remained in that location until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, Colonel. Let's turn for a little while to the topic of the command and control of the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to page 93 of 65 ter 2785, in the English, and page 97 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, and if you'll focus on the portion on the page in front of you, it's about halfway down the page. It begins, "vidite ..." There's a large paragraph. Thank you. Right there. And in the English, it's in the top paragraph and it begins, "You see ..." And you provide the investigators with an explanation of how command and control applies to the security and intelligence organs. And in your answer, you say that -- and I quote: "The corps commander commands me, and Tolimir controls me, or he runs me. And this is the professional line, the professional chain. These are the two lines that we're talking about when it comes to command and control." Can you explain for the Trial Chamber what you mean when you say "The corps commander commands me, but General Tolimir runs me"?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, security organs of the former JNA worked in accordance with the rules of security organs of the former JNA. The rules decidedly state, I don't have the rules here, so I cannot tell you which item it is within the rules, but the rules say that intelligence -- that is to say, security organs are subordinated to the commander of unit which they are a part of, and that professionally speaking, they are controlled by the immediately superior security organ. To clarify, within a corps command, I was commanded by the corps commander in war time. The corps commander is - let me put it that way - the lowest instance which has a full overview and a full insight into the work of security organs. That is to say, that he has a right to have an insight into counter-intelligence tasks of a security organ, which a brigade commander, for instance, does not have. In war time, the corps commander approves the implementation of secret working methods for security organs. In peacetime, an army commander would do that. That was the level in question. The corps commander would also assess me in the professional sense. It wouldn't be Mr. Tolimir, but, rather, the corps commander. That's command. So I am obliged to perform the tasks and duties which are assigned to me by the commander. But there is something specific I need to say. The former JNA, in security sense, trained unit commanders so that future brigade or regiment commanders came to the intelligence educational centre in Pancevo and they listened to lectures about working with security organs and on control with security organs. Likewise, brigade commanders at Command Staff academies, and these are all people who had graduated from these academies because it is a higher level than the basic academy, they were also given lectures by security organs by command and control in terms of security organs, and they could see the book rule of security organs. Other officers, officers of any rank who were outside of the security service and were not at the brigade commander or corps commander level, were not allowed to have an insight into the rule-book of security organs. That was the command element. As for control of security organs by the immediately superior organs, in this case, it was Tolimir, in relation to me, or Beara in relation to me, that is professional guidance in discharging counter-intelligence and security tasks and resolving related issues. General Tolimir and Colonel Beara were exceptionally professional, in terms of security service. This is undoubted. But, in general, the superior security organ is considered to be more educated, more intelligent, more experienced than the subordinate one and that it can properly guide him in discharging counter-intelligence tasks and resolving counter-intelligence problems. These were the two lines that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. Excuse me, for interrupting you, Mr. Prosecutor, at this juncture. Witness, I did understand the difference you explained between the task of a corps commander and those of a brigade commander. I saw that a corps commander has a complete overview of the counter-intelligence activities, which is not true for a brigade commander. But I can't understand why a brigade commander should not have a complete overview of the situation. If we remember that counter-intelligence work is to know what happens in the opposite camp. A brigade commander has to fight the enemy facing them. So, in your view, he doesn't need to know what is happening in the enemy's camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you finished?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I just want to know why a brigade commander cannot have a complete overview and insight into counter-intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The security organs' rule-book is defined in such a way that the corps commander may know this, whereas a brigade commander may not. It is believed that a brigade commander is a lower command level, which does not need to know this. It was a misunderstanding. Counter-intelligence tasks are not just what you mentioned; that is to say, collecting information about the enemy. That's a task for the intelligence service. The counter-intelligence tasks are, for example, implementing secret working methods, focussing on a specific person who is working within the brigade command. In order to apply these methods, the corps commander is informed about that but the brigade commander isn't, because, according to the rule, the brigade commander is not the level which needs to know this, regardless of the fact that this is a person from his own brigade. And why is that so? We had cases in which the brigade commander would become aware of the method which is applied to a person who is being observed, in intelligence terms, from his own unit, which is quite bad because not even all brigade commanders were mature enough for this position, even though they may have been discharging it. And another thing. There were brigade commanders to whom one could tell; that is to say, this could have been applied selectively. They could have been told that something was being done in their environment; that is to say, in their unit or something like that. But the remaining part of the answer to your question is this: The rule from the rule-book decidedly defined that a corps commander is one level and that the brigade commander is another level which cannot know this. And I just tried to elaborate that. And brigade commanders were aware of this, that they were not allowed to know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Therefore, a brigade commander is just somebody who carries out orders and doesn't need to know what is being designed at the level of the Main Staff or at the level of the corps. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, Your Honour. This is the principle probably an all armies that a certain command level also has a specific level of information. Not everyone can have the same amount of information. I think that is perhaps the best explanation to it all, including your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. I needed a clarification, just to understand something that you said in -- at page 41, line 1 to 4, on today's transcript. And you stated there: "I also believe, since the situation there was stable, it worked in the East Bosnia Corps, as well as in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, so all those corps which stayed within their areas. Since they didn't need to move, they probably could still rely on the Neven system." My question is: Do you know for a fact that the Neven system worked, as you state, in the East Bosnia Corps, or are you just supposing because they did not move? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that I may reduce that, because I said probably, so it's an assumption, which is most probably correct because they didn't move, so that means there was no reason to interrupt the system. They were simply stable and they were in their own area, as opposed to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This relates also to the Drina Corps, as Mr. Thayer was asking you, in addition; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yes. Because when I was listing the corps, I just mentioned the others as examples. I didn't list them all. I suppose it was also the Drina Corps because they were also not moving. And the counter-intelligence group, for example, was also using the same system, and probably there were not any changes of that kind within their remit because they were in Banja Luka, I mean, all the corps and units which stayed in their zones of responsibilities and had no need to leave their command posts at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, I want to follow up on Honourable Judge Mindua's question about the brigade commanders not being privy to certain information that the corps commander was privy to. The -- and I think you've spoken about this in your interview and you touched upon it in the Popovic trial a little bit. When we -- or when you speak about the brigade commander not being allowed to know certain information, are we talking about, in specific, counter-intelligence information first? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, brigade commanders could not know counter-intelligence information. They could if, as I earlier said, they were mature, responsible, as I could say. So they could be -- said something general. But there were all other security issues that the security organ was obliged to inform them about. It was obliged to inform them about all other security problems which arose within the unit and in the territory. As I say, the counter-intelligence problems were a very narrow area, especially when a specific secret working method was applied on someone from the brigade command or someone who was a member of the brigade. All other security information was something that the security organ had to be relayed to a brigade commander, just as I had to inform the corps commander about it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I think you spoke earlier in your testimony about having to protect the commander from people that might have been infiltrating his inner circle, so to speak. So when we speak of this counter-intelligence information that the brigade commander couldn't know about, are we really talking about internal threats, as opposed to external threats? Is that fair to -- fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: These were both of those threats, as you have phrased your question. Most often, we talked about threats coming from within because that was closest and also most frequent and most painful eventually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Sorry once again, Mr. Prosecutor. Your follow-up question after the question I raised forces me into uncertainty once again. Because, Witness, in the army, we have a principle, the one of a single command. And I believe that in the JNA, as well as in the VRS, it was very well applied. The JNA officers were among the best, at least the best trained, officers in the world. My problem now is at the level of a brigade. Because you said that at all levels a commander commands, whilst in the professional chain you have the superior who controls.
