So here we have a brigade with a commander who commands, and we have an officer of the security or counter-intelligence department who hides something from his own commander and is bound to undertake actions sooner or later, actions that the commander is not aware of. So what happens if you have an officer under the orders of a brigade commander who might wish to start something without his commander not knowing about it, and then refuses, because he has not been informed of the actions? Have you come across such cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have not fully understood your question. In particular, the last part of the question. Can you please be more specific?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will be more specific. At the brigade level, you have a brigade commander with, under his orders, a counter-intelligence department officer. The latter would like to undertake a task, and this is refused. This is not authorised by the brigade commander because he has not been informed. Could such a case occur or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now I have understood the question. It did occur, and, as a consequence, once, or, perhaps, twice, we received instructions from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska on command and control of security organs. This document was produced precisely as a consequence of this internal misunderstanding, or to be more precise, misunderstanding between a brigade commander and the security organ, in terms of the duties of the security organ. This document warned about such occurrences as there were cases that, for example, the mail, which is indecent in private life to open somebody else's mail -- that brigade commanders opened the mail for security organs which was addressed specifically and personally to the security organ. There were such cases. There were cases where they did not allow the use of the command code to send security reports. There were such cases, too, and, therefore, you are right in what you said. Let me also try to clarify something about your previous question and also the question of Mr. Prosecutor. To repeat, the security organ in the brigade had to, was obliged to, relay all security information relating to the territory and the unit that was collected. The commander had to be presented all this information and informed about it. But, by contrast, there was no such obligation relating to the counter-intelligence information. As the chief in the corps, I had the right to go and meet with the brigade commander and inform him about something if I believed that he needed to know that. Of course, I would have done that after talking and obtaining approval of the corps commander. I'm not sure if I managed now to clarify some of the issues following from the questions which you have asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's much clearer now. Thank you very much. I understand much better now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So using the example that you and Honourable Judge Mindua just shared, could it have been the case that you had a security chief of a brigade, an assistant commander for security in a brigade, who is the brigade commander's subordinate, privy to information because of his status as a security officer, that the brigade commander does not himself know, such that the brigade commander's subordinate knows something and you know something about counter-intelligence issues but the brigade commander himself doesn't know?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was possible. Because, as I told you, this is what is set out in the security organs' rule-book, and we had to work in accordance with these rules. When answering the Honourable Judge, I said earlier that it was possible for me to meet with a brigade commander and inform him about a certain problem, if I was sure that he was mature enough and that he would not abuse this information in any way. There were brigade commanders who believed that they were the subject of interest of security organs and that security organs were dealing with them, and that was why they did the things that I mentioned earlier. And essentially they were commanders whose account from the war should have been looked at. That was why they expressed concern or they had doubts that they were the subject of investigation which was not correct. There was no need for them to act in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So from -- from what I understand from your answer to Honourable Judge Mindua's question, the fact that a subordinate of a brigade commander has information that he is not sharing with his commander, doesn't necessarily cripple that commander's ability to command. Because, as you said, the commander is still receiving all of the other security and intelligence information which he needs to exercise his command as a commander. Is that a fair way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you have made an excellent observation. Essentially this was not information, at least that is my view, that might have a significant impact on command and control in a unit. If there was information that would have a significant impact on the command and control of a unit, then somebody would have reacted immediately. For example, the enemy activity which may have occurred within a unit would have been eliminated immediately. But it had to be proved first that it was really enemy activity. So while the time when this was monitored, the brigade commander would not feel the activity so it wouldn't have an impact or affect his orders, the use of the unit. He wouldn't feel the activity was ongoing, nor was he even aware of it. I'm not sure if I was precise enough and clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to the command and control of the security organs. You had spoken about the command line versus the professional or expert line wherein General Tolimir ran you professionally. I want to save a little bit of time and just quote to you from your interview. And this is at page 87 of the English and page 91 of the B/C/S. And, again, you, I think, encapsulate in your answer, to some degree, what we are talking about. You said: "It is the corps commander to whom I am responsible for my activities, but when it comes to the expert side of the whole thing, it's Colonel Beara who is in charge of me and the second superior officer is General Tolimir." And then you say for intelligence matters: "I had to report to Colonel Salapura as well, and, naturally, again, Tolimir above him." Let me just pause for a moment and make sure that is getting translated to you and that you understand what I've quoted from.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was interpreted correctly. What I said then is something that I stand by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And it wasn't the case that you would have to report twice: Once to Salapura; and then once to General Tolimir, was it, sir? You reported to Colonel Salapura and then he would, in turn, report to Tolimir; is that correct? Or did it work some other way?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in principle, it was so. As a subordinate of the security administration, I was supposed to draft reports sent to that one single place. And then both administrations, security and intelligence administrations, draft a report for Tolimir and for the commander of the Main Staff. This was according to the rules. At the time when we were still joined, then both knew all information, of course. Later on, when the functions were separated, they exchanged information.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's go to page 107 of the English in 65 ter 2785, please. And we'll need to look at page 112 in the B/C/S. And, again, this is on the topic of command and control within the security and intelligence organs in the VRS. In the English, we'll be looking at the bottom of the page; and, as well, in the B/C/S. Colonel, if you would focus, please, on the paragraph that begins, "Ne ne" at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in the English, it's the paragraph that begins, "You see ..." You say here in your answer: "I cannot issue orders to the brigade commanders. I can issue orders to the security organs, to be careful about the communications through phone lines and other types of communications ... I could inform the brigade commanders to sign an information or a document that would go to the brigade commanders, to address them in my capacity as the chief of security in order to make them more serious in respect of the security situation. But I could never say, I order to them." My first question is: Has this transcript accurately reflected your explanation; and if it has, can you just explain to the Trial Chamber what you're talking about here, please?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is correct and accurate. It reflects what I said. As far as I could see here, we were discussing information sent from the Main Staff concerning the interception of electronic communication and radio reconnaissance conducted by the enemy. That information was probably a summary of all the information that security departments from the corps sent to the security administration. And based on that, the summary was made and then the information disseminated. What was it all about? Well, it was a sort of warning to pay more attention to protect secrecy in radio communication. In other words, to prevent leaking secret military information by way of radio communication. In a way, it seems that people became too lax, having forgotten that their radio systems they used did not all have encryption. They forgot that what they said could be openly heard, including all information they referred to. It was customary at the time in the army to use the so-called TKT documents. This was an abbreviation for secret telecommunication code which basically consisted of a code list, including terms and words that were important, as well as numbers. Obviously this was not used, and secret military information was leaked. That is why this information notice was sent, and it was signed by Boric, the corps commander. He sent it to the brigade commanders. As the security service, we realised there was a security issue to deal with. One of the ways of dealing with it was to send an order by the corps commander to the brigade commanders to pay attention and to undertake measures. That is why I wanted to stress that I was not a superior to the brigade commanders. It was the corps commander who could do this. I was not authorised by the law, and I was not their superior. I could only propose to the corps commander to draft a document of this kind which would then be sent by way of his orders to his subordinate commanders. This is what I wanted to explain in the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in this example that you've told us about from -- from your interview, you said that -- and I quote: "I can issue orders to the security organs to be careful about the communications through phone lines and other types of communications." Can the tell the Trial Chamber what other types of orders you, in your capacity as security chief, could issue?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: As the chief of security, I could issue orders to my subordinate security organs, or directives. To say that I could order would make it part of command, but I could tell them to do something by applying a specific method in specific circumstances. Then I could ask for information to be passed to me on, say, an incident of theft in the unit if it was of any importance. It included everything that fell within the scope of activities of security organs. Since at the corps level, we had more information as compared to the levels of brigades, we frequently received information from the security administration that in the territory of a specific brigade there was somebody doing something for the enemy, or that there was a radio device there. We would then include that in our instructions to the chief of security in the brigades to verify that. Once verified, we would then propose measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what ability did the subordinate - to whom this directive from you was issued - have to disregard your directive going down to that subordinate organ?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't think he could ignore it or disregard.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And why not, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Because it was a superior/subordinate relationship. And we all know what consequences one may face if refusing to carry out an order in times of war. Also, well, how should I put it? This relationship between me and my subordinate security organs was not a very firm or inflexible relationship. It was a matter of agreement and a matter of discussion on how to deal with a certain problem. It's a specific job which includes different work methods to, say, the use of a gun, rifle, or a tank. This is rather specific. It is primarily a mental task, and it is specific in that regard. I don't recall having had such situations in which anyone from my subordinate security organs refused. There were other situations in which some brigade security personnel had to be removed from their posts, but those situations were different. This is what I can tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to follow up on your answer, Colonel, you said: "And we all know what consequences one may face if refusing to carry out an order in times of war." What were the consequences, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, unfortunately, at the time, we had no court-martial during the war. This is my personal remark. But it would entail removal from duty, detention, prosecution. Those were the measures that were applied in war time. There was no time to place any other measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, page 57, line 1, it seems that the answer of the witness was not interpreted as precisely as we would wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, could you please clarify with the witness if this interpretation reflects correctly what he said to your answer [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, on my LiveNote, Mr. President, the answer is: "I don't think he could ignore it or disregard." I'm not sure if that is the line in question. If it is, it is what I heard. So I'm not sure what the -- what the alleged error is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, could you explain your concern?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am unable to recall the precise answer. In interpretation, it seems that some terms were missing or some terms were extra. I don't think the witness mentioned the command relationship in that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well -- Mr. President, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To avoid any problems, please put your question again to the witness, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right. I'll start from the bottom of page 56, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My question was, Colonel: What ability did your professional subordinate have to disregard your directive, going down to that subordinate organ.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I said that they weren't supposed to. Perhaps that expression was missing from the translation. As for the other terms, that's something that I can accept. They fully reflect what I intended to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when you said, "We all know the consequences of disregarding an order in a time of war," Colonel let's -- I'll be frank, if not a little vulgar, here in the Court. Did you ever hear of anybody being shot for failing to carry out an order in a time of war?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: No. I've never heard of anything like that. That is why I specifically mentioned summary court-martials.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when you say you've never heard of anything like that, are you referring to war in which you were participating only, or is it the case that you've never heard of soldiers being shot in a time of war? Let's just go back to conflicts in the 20th century, don't have to go further than that. Have you heard of that method being applied to soldiers in a time of war, who failed to carry out an order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Thayer, you're going a bit too far to refer to all possible wars in the 20th century. You should restrict your questions to the relevant period of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on, Mr. President. Let's look at page 83, if we could, of this interview. And it will be pages 86 to 87 in the B/C/S. And in the B/C/S, we'll be starting at the very bottom of the page, please. The paragraph beginning, "malo ..." Okay. Have you had a chance to read that? And if we could go to the next page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I see -- I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can go to the next page, top of the page, in B/C/S. And we are at the top of the page in English. You state, Colonel, that: "General Tolimir could also order us to do things through his own chain, with his own signature." And then you're asked: "Tolimir could order forces, actually?" And your answer is: "Security organs and the intelligence organs." And the follow-up question is: "Including the military police?" And your answer is: "Yes. So he could." Can you explain a little bit what you're talking about here in this answer, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in this part of the interview, we were discussing who had the right to assign what documents and who could sign for someone else. Specifically, we were discussing who could sign a document for Mladic or who could sign documents within my command. I said then that General Tolimir could issue an order to the security and intelligence organs as their superior officer. He could also issue orders to the military police following an approval of the Main Staff commander. This is something I need to add to what I said then. When it comes to the use of a military police unit in combat, this is -- this would be a situation in which he required an approval. As for the training and equipping units of the military police, in such instances, he could issue direct orders because equipping and training a unit was part of the work of the security organ. I don't know whether at the level of the Main Staff there was a MP unit. If there was one, it was probably part of the protection regiment. If we go back to the issue of orders, that was the sense of my answer then, and I just tried to explain it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You gave us an example a few moments ago of issuing a directive, to use that term, and you've also used the term "order," although I understand you want to distinguish your role from that of a commander. But you gave an example a little while ago of a directive in connection with proper use of communications. Can you provide the Trial Chamber with any other examples of where you would issue directives or orders down your subordinate chain.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Basically, as I said, I could issue a directive, or order, to those who were in the security department as part of the corps command and to my subordinate security organs in the commands of brigades, regiments, and independent battalions. Following the corps commander's approval, I could issue an order to the military police unit, or, to be more specific, to the MP battalion, as regards training, equipment, and similar issues. I could also suggest or propose to the commander how to use the military police unit, but it was his sole discretion to order any such use. While the intelligence and security organs were still merged, they could put such proposals to the commanders to use reconnaissance units, although it was more under the competence or in co-ordination with the Chief of Staff of the corps because it was usually the Chiefs of Staff of corps and brigades who were in charge of reconnaissance units at troop level. In other words, as the security organ, I had no right to order to anyone in the MP battalion or to order any brigade or battalion commander. I was only a superior officer to those who were in the security and intelligence departments, and such departments had five to six people. And I was also a superior to those who were placed in the different brigades and regiments.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now in the -- I think we're pretty much at the break, but if I could just ask one more question, and we'll be done with this topic, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You said in your interview and this is at page 97 of the English and pages 101 to 102 of the B/C/S. You said that the corps' military police battalions had to report to the Main Staff military police service. That's then-Colonel Keserovic. They also had to report to you as the security chief and they had to report to the corps commander. I just wanted to ask you, number one, is -- is that accurately reflected in the -- in the transcript, that the corps' military police battalions had to report to all three of those levels?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: It is correct, what I said then, and what you just said now. In military police battalions, you had the duty military police service. It would compose reports about the events and military police duties which the military police battalion had carried out during the day. These reports were sent to the corps command, to the operative duty officer, where all reports from units were collated. Then by telegram, they would be sent to the security administration directly and to us, security organs, for our information. Why were they sent directly there? So that we wouldn't duplicate reports. So that we wouldn't, as security organs, send reports about the military police unit. That was why it was done in this way. And this is the system that we inherited from before the war. I think it is also regulated in the rule-book for military police. If I need to repeat, one was the corps operational duty officer, the other one was the chief of the department for military police duties at the security administration because it was at the level of Keserovic where all the information about the activities of military police were collected --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the witness please repeat the third addressee.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And there were three that we were referring to and we just need to pick up, for the record, the third addressee. We just didn't catch it on the record. Who was the third?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: The corps command, the corps security department, and the military police department at the security administration of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I see we're a couple minutes beyond the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We must have our second break now, and we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon again to you and to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about one topic about which the Trial Chamber has heard some testimony, and that has to do with the combat readiness analyses which were conducted in the VRS. You spoke about it during your OTP interview, and just to save a little bit of time, if you could just tell the Trial Chamber a little bit about what these combat readiness analyses were all about, what their purpose was and how the VRS went about conducting them?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the analysis of combat readiness was a planned activity which was carried out once or twice per year at the level of the VRS. The analysis was preceded by an order. I'm talking about the corps command now. An order to make the analysis, which the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska would submit to corps commands. This order precisely specified the issues which the analysis needed to deal with. On receiving the document - and I will be talking about the process - I hope I understood the character of your question properly. You want me to talk about the procession of analysing combat readiness. On receiving the document, the corps command would compose its own document on the basis of the one received from the Main Staff, and it would send it to brigade commands and its subordinate units, brigades and regiments, of course with a deadline, which allowed the corps command to have sufficient time to make its own analysis. Once the brigade commander has received such an order, they would make their own orders and send it down to battalion commands, and also give a deadline which would allow them to collate all the reports in a timely fashion and submit their own report to the corps command. It was a process, beginning with the moment when you received the order to make the analysis of combat readiness from the Main Staff to the moment when the order was disseminated through the lower units. The contrary process, after informing brigade commands, there would be a brigade command meeting at which, collectively, each in his own area of responsibility, people would provide answers to certain questions and make an analysis of combat readiness for the corps level. This analysis of combat readiness would be taken by the corps commander to the Main Staff at the specific ordered time. He would take it there, and he would defend it at the Main Staff. He would defend it verbally. Regardless of the fact that it was composed in writing, he had to defend it. That is to say, he had to state verbally what the analysis included, what problems the unit has been facing, and how these specific problems were overcome. So, more or less, that was the process by which this analysis was made, if that is what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Indeed, thank you, Colonel. And was there specific input at the various levels, brigade and corps, by your organs, the security intelligence organs, into this analysis?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As part of the combat readiness analysis, the security organs and intelligence organs had their own points, their own questions. Security support and intelligence support, because, in addition to these supports, there was also morale support, logistical support, engineering, AVHO, and so on and so forth. So all the elements which command and control implies had to be included and answers had to be provided concerning each of these. Let me also emphasise another detail. When the brigade command made the analysis of combat readiness, a meeting would be held at which somebody from the brigade command would often be present. I apologise, I meant the corps command. Either the commander or his deputy would be present, and so would some other members of the command, of course. Likewise, when the corps made its own combat readiness analysis, usually somebody from the superior command, that is to say, from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, would attend the meeting. Sometimes it was the commander himself, if it was possible, and so on. That was the principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what was the essential purpose of these combat readiness analyses?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The essential purpose of any combat readiness analysis was to plan further combat operations. When we're talking about war time to see how ready any unit was, because through the analysis of combat readiness, you would get a picture of a unit, what it was like. Of course, if the analysis was realistic, what the unit was like, and whether it was ready to carry out combat operations or not. In other words, could you count on that unit when planning specific combat operations, actions and so on. That is the basic element.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's turn to another topic. In both your Popovic testimony, to some degree, and in your interview with the OTP, and the Trial Chamber heard a little bit of this in my summary this morning of your Popovic testimony, you spoke about when you met certain high-level VRS officers, such as Colonel Beara, then-Colonel Tolimir, and when General Mladic also worked with those officers before the war broke out. Do you recall telling us in the Popovic trial and the investigators during your interview about that topic?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I also remember my answers, which I will repeat now. Namely, by way of introduction, I said that I graduated from the academy in 1979 and, later on, I went to the Postina Garrison in Slovenia. That was where I was appointed. Around 1985 or 1986, I was redeployed to the Sibenik Garrison. I was already working for security organs at the time. I was their member. I met General Tolimir in Belgrade. I saw him for the first time in Belgrade when he was in the foreign languages school, together with my friend, the late Colonel Milan Stevilovic. That was when I saw him for the first time. I believe that he held the rank of major. Whether I was already in the military naval district at the time or was I still at the Postina Garrison, I'm not certain, but it was in 1985 or 1986. As for the naval Captain Beara, I met him in Sibenik. After I arrived there, and after I had been working there fore a while, perhaps one month, I'm not sure, the naval captain was touring and he was controlling the work of security organs at the military naval district Sibenik. And this district was responsible for the zone from Kornati, a part of Zadar. Kornati, as I said, Sibenik, all the way down to Ploce, if you are familiar with the coast, including all the islands such as Hvar, Brac, Solta, Lastovo, Vis, and so on. So it was quite a big area. And I note that because of your question why they gave one major and 50 soldiers, why I was important at the time, I was deputy chief of security for this whole territory. So naval Captain Beara arrived and he was, at the time, deputy chief of security of the military naval district, or navy, just to put it more simply. He was the deputy for counter-intelligence affairs. That was our first contact. Later on, we also had other contacts. More frequently, regularly, it was professional and sometimes we met in Sibenik and on other occasions in Split. Later on, I used to see General Tolimir in Split. At the time he was already chief of the counter-intelligence group of the Naval Military District. Later, I used to see him in Knin, especially after I had been released from detention because at the same time General Tolimir was chief of the security department in the Knin Corps. Let me repeat, General Mladic was at the time the Chief of Staff of the Knin Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So, it is it fair to say that, in addition to yourself, Colonel Beara, then-Colonel Tolimir, and General Mladic all knew each other, to some degree, worked with each other, during this time in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: You see, it was a short period. Until I was taken prisoner, I had been in Sibenik, not in Knin. Tolimir had been in Knin, and Beara had been in Split. After I was released from custody, I came to Knin, and I was appointed the chief of the counter-intelligence group of the corps, and Tolimir became my first superior. I believe that at the time Beara was down in Boka Kotorska on the Montenegrin coast where navy command had moved from Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And when the JNA broke up, can you tell the Trial Chamber, among the various ethnicities of the officer corps that made up the JNA -- among the various ethnicities, which ethnicity had the greatest number of professional officers within the JNA and which had the least? If you could just provide the Trial Chamber with some idea. I think you talked about that in your interview. If you could just share that with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the then-corps command, there were most Serbs, officers and non-commissioned Serbs, specifically Serbs who were born in Bosnia and Herzegovina. All those who had not been born in Bosnia-Herzegovina left the territory of the corps, its zone, on the 19th of May. The corps had not existed yet at the time but they left the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I could interrupt you. I see a problem in the transcript which happens from time to time. I used the word core, in English, c-o-r-e, meaning the officer -- I beg your pardon, no, no. Let me start over again. Let me follow up on what you just said Colonel. You referred specifically to the corps which had not existed at the time. My question is a little bit more general. When the JNA broke up -- can you just give the Trial Chamber an idea of when the VRS was formed, the officer class instead of -- I don't want to use the word "corps" because I don't mean a specific corps, as in East Bosnia Corps, Knin Corps, but in terms of a group of officers from the JNA, can you just give the Trial Chamber an idea of the percentage of ethnicity, who had the most highly trained -- most of the highly trained officers, who had the least. And then I'll ask -- I'll move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: I just said these were Serbs as the most numerous, and, more specifically, Serbs born in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If we talk in more general terms, the general situation, I can tell that you in the Knin Corps, there were also officers who were not just Serbs but also Muslims, including Mr. Dudakovic, who was one of the officers there, the Muslim general. There were Croatian officers. There were soldiers who were ethnic Albanian from Kosovo and so on. That was the situation in Knin. In our corps, in addition to Serbs, there was a small number of Croats and Muslims, both among the officers and among the soldiers. The military police unit, the military police battalion, also included some soldiers who were Muslims and an officer who was a Croat. But at the corps command, we had one officer who was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you testified in the Popovic trial that you held Colonels Beara and Popovic in high esteem, and the Trial Chamber has the record of what you said about them as officers. You also told us in the 2004 OTP interview about how you regarded General Tolimir as an officer. And if you could share with the Trial Chamber your personal assessment, as you did in 2004, with the Trial Chamber. And rather than put it up on the screen, I'll just ask you to share that with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said then and I repeat today that I have had a high opinion about the personality of naval Captain Beara, who, at the time before the war and later during the war, was a figure of authority for security organs. Undoubtedly, he was highly professional and a man who knew how to control security organs. I can say the same thing for General Tolimir. He is very knowledgeable, a great expert, and we had to learn many things from him. We had to and we needed to. And regardless of the situation that he is in now, Tolimir, and also Beara and Popovic -- Popovic was my subordinate. You noted there that it was at my proposal that he was appointed as the chief of security in the Drina Corps because I was the one who was supposed to go there. That was one of the possible combinations. But I asked General Tolimir not to transfer me to that part of the Bosnia-Herzegovina because, by origin, that's where I'm from. I'm a native of that area, and I did not wish to go there because I could have come into conflict with some of my relatives, the closest and more distant relatives. Because you know how it is, sometimes some people think you are right, others think you are wrong, and I wanted to keep as far away from that as possible. So I stayed where I was. And at the time, Major Popovic, I think he was major, was a man who was working well, who was responsible, and who needed a higher position, and he couldn't get one in the 2nd Krajina Corps. So that is an explanation of sorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, and just so the record is clear, do you remember approximately what year that was that you recommended Popovic for that position?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, the Drina Corps was the last of these corps that was established. Was it late 1992 or early 1993? I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. For my last couple of questions, Colonel, I'd like to go back to your interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 2785. We'll be going to page 95 in the English; page 99 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, we'll be focussing about in the middle of the page where you're asked who commanded the 410th, referring to the 410th Intelligence Centre. And in English, that's at the very top of the page. If you would, just take a moment to read this section.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we'll need to go down just a little bit more in the B/C/S just to catch the very bottom. Now you were asked -- and, again, this goes back to the issue of command and control that we were talking about before. You were asked who Colonel Knezevic reported to. And you answered that he reported first to Salapura and then Tolimir. And you clarify that Knezevic could go directly to Tolimir if Salapura was not present, but as a matter of principle he had to go to Salapura first and then Salapura would inform Tolimir. You were then asked the question: "Is there any reason you can think of where there would be any secrets from General Tolimir, any intelligence or security-related matter?" And your answer was: "In my case, there definitely wasn't any. I can't tell you anything about other organs, but, in principle, there shouldn't have been any, because also, General Tolimir would have surely found out if something had been kept a secret. And in that case, I wouldn't like to be in the skin of the person who tried to keep secrets from him." Now, I asked you about this passage in the last trial. What I want to ask you today is: Can you tell the Trial Chamber why it was so important not to keep secrets from General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: First of all, as for myself, there were not any such situations. And I believe that concealing any information or an attempt to conceal them may have caused harm, not just personal harm to the security organ that would do such a thing, but it would be harmful for the assessment of the situation, a specific situation, perhaps. It is certain that on the basis of the information which he received, General Tolimir made counter-intelligence assessments all the time and security assessments as well, because that is the main task of any security organ. Should it happen that an information which is available was not presented to him, I don't think that ever happened but I think that the consequence would be that he wouldn't have a full picture about something, an event, or something similar. As for what I said here, you quoted about the 410th and all that. Who did Colonel Cedo Knezevic report to? I said that he could say something directly to Tolimir, in case Salapura was absent. He could have done that, but that does not mean that Salapura would be bypassed. It was just a way to relay information more quickly. Perhaps that caused some doubt on part of the investigator, and so he asked the question whether it happened and what would have happened if any information was concealed from Tolimir. No, that did not happen. And that was why Cedo reported to Salapura and Salapura normally reported to Tolimir as his superior. I'm not sure if I now managed to explain this a little bit to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I think that does clarify the matter. Now, in the event -- and let's just follow up with what you mentioned last there. In the event that Colonel Knezevic couldn't get a hold of Colonel Salapura and had to go directly to General Tolimir, would it have been the practice that Colonel Knezevic would at the earliest opportunity that he had to contact Colonel Salapura, would then also inform Colonel Salapura, even though he had already talked to General Tolimir, in Colonel Salapura's absence?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In principle, that could have happened, and it probably did. There was no harm in conveying the same thing twice. Perhaps Salapura received such information from Tolimir in the meantime and then Knezevic would inform him by just repeating it. But we as subordinates don't know whether our superiors communicated with each other and when. So just in case, we, again, report the same thing to the first superior, the immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, for my last question on -- on this topic, Colonel. When you were serving -- again, we're talking about the corps level. When you were the corps chief of the security department or, indeed, when the two departments, security and intelligence, were unified, when you were chief of security and intelligence affairs, how important was it for you to know everything that was going on? You've spoken about how a brigade commander didn't necessarily have to know everything that was going on, but you've told us previously that the corps commander had to know everything that was going on and you had to know everything that was going on. Why was it important for you as that corps officer to know everything that was going on?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is very important to know everything that was -- that is going on in the corps so as to be able to produce an adequate, proper security assessment. I was supposed to be informed if, say, a unit abandoned its positions or refused to take food or refused to take up a position. These are all security issues which may imply losing ground, victims and casualties among our ranks, or our soldiers being captured and equipment lost. This is just a segment of the reasons why we needed to know everything that was going on. I also had to receive such information from my subordinate security organs, in order to inform the corps commander appropriately. It was on the basis of that information, provided by the security service, and some other information, the commander conducted his daily procedure of command and control over his units. I had to know it all so that I could report it to my superior command. They needed to know what some things were about and what their nature was, as well as whether it could reflect on the morale of the unit, its combat readiness, et cetera, although it was up to the corps commander to assess combat readiness and morale. In that regard, it was very important to have information because by knowing you prevent being surprised, caught unawares.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what were the consequences of secrets were kept from you [sic]?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: When it happened, and it rarely did, well, you know what our people say, that liars don't stand their ground too long. Truth always outs. Of course, regulations are one thing, and practice is another. If I had to remove a chief of security in a brigade for such an omission, there were no substitutes, there were no people you could choose from to replace him. So, for the most part, when there were serious omissions or infractions, people were removed from their positions and criminal reports submitted. And in cases when it involved information which could not immediately or significantly affect the situation at the front line or combat readiness, then we usually resorted to the disciplinary and advisory measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And why was it so important for General Tolimir in his position as assistant commander for security and intelligence to know everything that was going on, not to have secrets kept from him?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: An answer to that question could be brought down to what I said a moment ago, as to why it was important for me to know. The same applies to Tolimir's level, which was higher up. He also had to inform the commander and the command with its staff with what was going on and what the situation was like in certain parts of our territory and in certain units. Based on his information, the commander made decisions and assessments on whether there would be any combat engagement and where. Basically, it all boiled down to whether you can engage a particular unit in combat or not. If you can, how; and if you cannot, why. And what can you do to enable that unit to engage in combat. In a time of war, nothing else is as important.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I have just one more question for you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could stay on page 95 in the English. If we could scroll all the way down. And we'll need to go to page 100 in the B/C/S of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, if you could focus on the next couple of questions you were asked that have to do with places of worship being destroyed. Just take a moment and read that section, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in English, it starts at the bottom third and continues onto the next page. And we'll move on in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You were asked about mosques being blown up and destruction of homes and so forth. And you answered that: "Especially at the beginning of the war, religious buildings of all confessions and all three sides were being destroyed. I'll be honest with you, it wasn't reported ... it was a normal occurrence." And you were asked if the Main Staff knew that this was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we have to go to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And your answer was: "Well, they visited the territory, they'd see that the mosque wasn't there, the Catholic church wasn't there, the Orthodox church wasn't there. It was a well-known thing. Everybody did it. We did it. The Muslims did it. The Croats did it. The locations where these religious buildings were preserved are rare." My question to you, Colonel, simply is: Do you stand by what you said in your 2004 interview about houses of worship of all religions were destroyed by the other side during the war?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This was so on all three sides. There were very few settlements in which an enemy army went that managed to preserve their religious buildings. As I said, it was a standard occurrence. There was a lot of fear on all sides and -- well, what can I tell you? It is sad. I said so then. It is sad that many historical monuments were destroyed. Many of them were religious buildings. It's a sad thing, and I was very much against that. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, we're at the end of my time. And I'm at the end of my examination. And I thank you again for your insight and experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thayer. You're just in time before we adjourn for the day. Mr. Tolimir, you may commence your cross-examination tomorrow. We have to adjourn. Let me remind you that the -- that there's no permission to have contact about the content of your testimony to either party during the break. We adjourn and resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 2nd day of June, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
